rows.title: Monetary Policy
rows.figure: BoE hiked to 4.00% (8–1; Mann for +50bp); Fed Dec hike ~80%; ECB Dec ~89%; BoJ Dec ~80%; BoC Dec ~56%; RBNZ Dec <50%
rows.read: The Bank of England raised rates and hinted at more, joining most big central banks that still lean toward higher rates. Fed officials kept arguing for a December hike, and European Central Bank President Christine Lagarde kept hers open without promising it. With these moves expected, currencies react to hints about the next step.

rows.title: Growth
rows.figure: US jobless claims 189K (fcst 197K); Q3 productivity +3.6%, unit labour costs −0.7%; German factory orders +4.4% Sep (fcst +4.8%)
rows.read: The US job market stays firm, with very few layoffs, and workers are producing more per hour, which lets firms grow without pushing up prices. German factories recovered part of a deep August slump. Friday's US and Canadian jobs figures are the next big read.

rows.title: Inflation
rows.figure: Brent ~$97.9 (+3.5%); US unit labour costs −0.7% Q3; BoE sees UK CPI near 5% by mid-2027; euro-area CPI 4.0% Oct
rows.read: Oil bounced back after new tanker attacks, so the energy push on prices has not gone away. In the US, falling labour costs per unit of output ease the risk that wages keep inflation high. The Bank of England now expects UK inflation to climb further next year, which is why it is still raising rates.

rows.title: Risk Sentiment
rows.figure: Nasdaq ~−5%, S&P 500 ~−4%, chip index ~−10%, VIX +60% (late session); USD/JPY 157.82 (−0.4%); AUD/USD 0.6935 (−1.0%); gold $4,124 (+1.6%)
rows.read: A sharp selloff in US chip and AI stocks turned markets fearful, wiping out the gains that followed Tuesday's election. Money went to the yen, gold and Treasury bonds, while the Australian and New Zealand dollars fell most. Whether this fear lasts is now a bigger driver than any single data release.

rows.title: Terms of Trade
rows.figure: Brent $97.94 (+3.5%), WTI $90.64 (+2.8%); at least five ships hit near Hormuz since Sunday; Eurasia Group deal odds 10%
rows.read: Oil climbed back after more tankers were hit near the Strait of Hormuz and hopes for a US–Iran deal faded. That raises the energy bill again for importers like Japan and the euro area and gives exporters like Canada a little more income. Today the stock slump mattered more to those currencies than oil did.

rows.title: Positioning
rows.figure: CFTC Oct 27: funds strongly against CAD, against EUR (real money for), against NZD, for AUD (real money strongly against), strongly for gold (cut); new report Fri Nov 6
rows.read: Hedge funds hold their biggest bets against the Canadian dollar and also bet against the euro and the kiwi, while real money investors bet for the euro. Big bets on the yen and gold mean days like today, when both rose, reward the side that is already full. New figures arrive Friday afternoon.

rows.title: Fiscal
rows.figure: Canada Budget 2026 tabled Nov 5, 3:00 PM CT (PBO pre-budget deficit ~C$63.3B for 2026–27); Democrats control House and Senate; Fitch France A+ negative
rows.read: Canada tabled its federal budget with tax breaks for business investment and money for energy projects; the full borrowing figures are still being checked. A Democratic Congress makes President Trump's spending plans harder to pass, which trims support for the dollar. France's debt worries still weigh on the euro.
